messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ramesh Patel is a 53-year-old married man who now makes his living as a house painter, though when he speaks about himself he does so with a quiet sense that the life he is in is not the one he was meant to be living. He grew up in a region marked by war and, during one bombardment in civilian housing, he was trapped in a collapsed building after an explosion tore through the street. What stays with him most is not a coherent sequence so much as fragments: the sharp chemical smell of smoke, dust, and burning material; the concussive bang that seemed to erase thought; and the helplessness of being pinned down, unable to control his body or protect the people beside him. He remembers being twisted awkwardly under debris, waiting for another strike, and the grief of realizing that not everyone nearby would come out alive. Even now, when he tries to tell the story, it can sound unreal to him, as if it happened to someone else, until his body suddenly tightens and he feels himself back in that position.

In the years since immigrating to the United States, Ramesh built a steady routine with his wife and found reliable work painting apartments and small commercial spaces. The trouble is that the very environment of his work brings him into contact with what he cannot manage. The smell of paint thinner, solvents, dust from sanding, or a faint burning odor in an old building can hit him with immediate force. A dropped ladder, a slammed dumpster lid, or the pop of construction equipment makes him jolt violently. Most difficult of all are moments when he cannot fully control what is happening around him—working on scaffolding while other crews move unpredictably, or being in a cramped room while someone else shuts the door. In those moments he becomes intensely watchful, scanning for exits, muscles drawn tight, body poised as if danger is seconds away. The trigger is never just a reminder; it convinces him afresh that the world is dangerous and that he is no longer a man who can function the way he once did.

When these reminders hit, memory does not come back as ordinary recollection. He feels his body curl and brace exactly as it had under the rubble, shoulders hunched and breath held, as if the scene is happening in the present. Along with that comes a wave of overwhelming grief, less about a single image than about the human loss embedded in the event. Because the memory arrives with such force, he has come to believe it says something final about him: that whatever competence and purpose once defined him are gone, and that nothing in his current life carries real meaning. Those thoughts make the memories harder to place in the past. He goes over and over why it happened to him, trying to find an answer that would make the suffering feel less arbitrary, but the rumination only keeps the event mentally active and close.

Over months and years, Ramesh has organized his life around not being caught by these states. He keeps relentlessly busy, taking extra jobs, staying in motion, filling evenings with tasks so there is little empty time in which his mind might drift back. He avoids news coverage of war, bombings, or civilian casualties because he knows even a brief report can leave him tense for hours. Yet the harder he works to push it away, the more sensitized he seems to become. Exhausted from constant effort and already on guard, he startles at ordinary sounds on the job and becomes more attentive to smells, enclosed spaces, and any hint that control is slipping. His wife has noticed that he no longer sits through televised reports with her and often paces the house afterward if loud noises come from outside. At work he has started turning down interior renovation jobs in crowded buildings, telling clients he is booked when in fact he is afraid of how quickly he can be thrown back into that bodily memory.

What frightens Ramesh most is how self-confirming it all feels. The more alert and tense his body becomes, the more easily a smell or bang grabs him; the more often he is jolted into the past, the more convinced he is that danger is everywhere and that he has been permanently diminished. He has come to watch himself closely for signs of losing control, and that vigilance itself makes those situations stand out all the more. By the time he sought help, the immediate reason was practical as much as emotional: after freezing and dropping his brush when a compressor backfired at a job site, he went home shaken and told his wife he could not keep pretending this was just stress. He says he wants “some peace” and to feel useful again, but underneath that hope is a fear that the war has followed him permanently, and that if he stops keeping busy for even a moment, the grief and the body memory will take over completely.
